```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")

workdir <- file.path(tempdir(), "lints-article")
dir.create(workdir, showWarnings = FALSE)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = workdir)
```

This article is for authors who want to find problems in a project's
documents without rendering them: numbers typed into the prose, constructs
that will not parse, broken cross-references, figures without alt text.
After it you will be able to run the lints, read their findings, fix or
exempt each one, and tune the rules for a project.

```{r}
library(weft)
```

## What a lint is

A **lint** is a rule with a stable id. `lints()` reads every `.qmd` and
`.Rmd` in a project as text, runs nothing, and returns the **findings**: one
row for each place a rule matched, with its file, line and column, the rule,
a message that ends with the rule's number in the design, and a hint.

Every rule has a **tier**:

| Tier | What it is | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | a hard rule, decidable from the source | fails the commit, the render or `verify()` |
| 2 | a heuristic | listed for newly added lines by `changes()` and `verify()`; blocks nothing |
| 3 | a human read | the ranked list of `changes()`; never decided by weft |

`lint_rules()` lists every rule:

```{r}
lint_rules()[, c("id", "tier", "scope", "what")]
```

A rule's **scope** is `file` when it reads one document at a time, and
`project` when it reads them all, as cross-references do.

## Running the lints

This project has an empty `_weft.yml` and one document with several
problems:

```{r}
writeLines("", "_weft.yml")
writeLines(c(
  "---",
  "title: \"Survey\"",
  "---",
  "",
  "## Results {#sec-results}",
  "",
  "```{r}",
  "#| label: data",
  "n_sites <- 12",
  "```",
  "",
  "We visited 14 sites in 2023, and Site 4 was dry.",
  "Of these, `r 3 + 4` were above the trigger.",
  "Turbidity [rose | fell]{if=\"slope > 0\" .num}.",
  "All sites were sampled at `r n_sites` locations.",
  "Samples were filtered through [0.45 µm]{.weft-literal why=\"pore size set by the laboratory method\"} membranes.",
  "Discharge [rose | fell]{iff=\"q > 0\"} after the storm.",
  "See Figure 2 for the map.",
  "",
  "## Methods",
  "",
  "```{r}",
  "plot(1:3)",
  "```"
), "survey.qmd")
lints()
```

By default `lints()` runs the tier-1 rules over the whole project.
`lints(files = )` limits the report to some documents, `rules = ` names
rules by id, and `tier = 2` or `tier = 1:2` asks for the heuristics:

```{r}
lints(tier = 2)
```

## Typed numbers

The rule `numeral` is the centre of the lints. Every numeral in the prose
must be one of these:

- a computed value, `` `r knitr::inline_expr("n_sites")` ``;
- a value from the dictionary, `` `r knitr::inline_expr("dict$trigger")` ``;
- inside a `cite` span, because it is quoted from a source;
- inside a `.weft-literal` span or block, with a `why` that says why it is
  fixed.

A word whose first letter or digit is a digit is a numeral: "12", "45%",
"11-year", "3rd", "1990s". A word that starts with a letter is a name: "CO2",
"PM2.5". The rule reads the body, captions, the front-matter fields that
take constructs, `weft_str()` strings, and inline math, where an exponent or
a subscript is exempt.

The `.weft-literal` span in the example above is why "0.45" is not a
finding. Its `why` is the record: nothing else lists it.

Two settings in `_weft.yml` exempt more:

- `label_words`: words after which a number is a name, not a quantity, such
  as "Site" in "Site 4". The list starts empty. `label_seed()` proposes
  candidates from the prose.
- `numeral_years: true` exempts a four-digit year from 1000 to 2999, a year
  range such as 2016-17, a decade and a possessive year. It is off by
  default, because a year in prose is often a choice that belongs in the
  dictionary.

```{r}
label_seed(min_count = 1)
writeLines(c("label_words: [Site]", "numeral_years: true"), "_weft.yml")
lints(rules = "numeral")
```

A number after a word Quarto can cross-reference ("Figure 2", "Table 3",
"Section 4") is never exempt: write a cross-reference such as `@fig-map`
instead.

When weft is adopted, a project's existing documents may hold hundreds of
typed numbers. The commit gate tolerates the ones already committed and
refuses only new ones, so adoption can be gradual. See
`vignette("gate", package = "weft")`.

## Literal values

A value made only of constants, such as `` `r knitr::inline_expr("3 + 4")` ``
or `{n="3"}`, renders, but it is a number typed in the source. The rule
`literal-value` finds it. Compute the number, put it in the dictionary, or
write it as a `.weft-literal` with its `why`.

The tier-2 rules `value-constant` and `value-format` list a numeric constant
inside a computation (other than 0 and 1) and a value that rounds in code
with `round()`, `format()` or `sprintf()`. Rounding in code skips weft's
formatters, so the value has no printed record and `round()` drops trailing
zeros.

## Construct errors

A **construct error** is a mistake in weft syntax that the scanner finds
without running R: a formatter on an `if` span, as in the example, the wrong
number of arms, two classes from one group, a `"` inside an attribute value,
an id defined twice. The rule is `construct`. A render stops at the first
construct error, and the commit gate refuses a changed document that holds
one, whatever `HEAD` held.

The rule `block-start` finds a line inside a span that Pandoc would read as
the start of a new block, which cuts the span in two.

## Checks that cannot fail

The rule `inert-check` finds a `claim()` check, or an `if` condition, with
no variable in it: `claim(x, TRUE)` or `if="1 > 0"`. Such a check cannot
fail, and such a condition always chooses the same arm, so neither checks
anything.

## Cross-references, citations and figures

| Rule | Finds |
|---|---|
| `xref` | a reference, such as `@fig-map` or a link to `#sec-x`, with no anchor anywhere in the project |
| `anchor-twice` | an anchor defined twice |
| `ref-label` | a span whose text is also a reference-link label in the document |
| `cite-key`, `citation-key` | a citation key that is not in the bibliography |
| `cite-bare` | a bare-form `cite` span whose key is not cited in the same block |
| `figure` | a figure with no label, caption or alt text |
| `table-caption` | a table with no caption |
| `section-anchor` | a heading with no `{#id}` |
| `chunk-label` | an executed chunk with no label |

A missing section anchor or chunk label matters because the ledger keys each
value on its section, and a stable anchor keeps that key stable when the
heading's words change.

## Project hygiene

| Rule | Finds |
|---|---|
| `engine` | a `.qmd` with constructs but no `engine: knitr` in its own front matter |
| `above-setup` | a construct above the chunk that calls `weft_setup()` |
| `dict-key` | `dict$key` for a key the dictionary does not hold |
| `dict-assign` | chunk code that assigns to `dict` |
| `tar-name` | `tar_read()` of a target the store does not hold |
| `tar-cache` | a chunk that reads a target and has `cache: true` |
| `file-link` | a link or image to a file that is not there |
| `config-place` | a `weft:` key in `_quarto.yml`, or a project setting in a document |
| `read` | a file that is not UTF-8 |

## Python, Julia and Observable

A document that mixes languages reaches prose through R. These rules find
the ways a value from another language goes wrong on the way.

| Rule | Tier | Finds |
|---|---|---|
| `guest-inline` | 1 | inline code in another language, such as `` `{python} depth` ``, in a document knitr knits: knitr does not run it, so it prints as code |
| `guest-call` | 1 | `r.fmt_num(` and the like in a Python chunk, which pass arguments through reticulate and can turn a Python integer into a wrong number; `from weft import fmt_num` is safe |
| `guest-read` | 2 | `py$n` in R chunk code, and `py_eval()`, `py_call()`, `julia_eval()` and the like in a value, which weft does not check; `py_value()` and `jl_value()` are the guarded reads |
| `ojs-value` | 2 | an inline `` `{ojs} total` `` or a `${total}` in an Observable `md` or `html` template, which the reader's browser computes after weft's checks have run |

The first two block a commit like any tier-1 finding. The `engine` rule
also says which engine Quarto would pick for a Python or Julia document
and what to write instead.

## Tier-2 heuristics

The tier-2 rules guess. Their findings are worth a look and never block
anything:

- `claim-word`: a quantifier, extreme or direction word ("all", "only",
  "largest", "rose") in a sentence with a value, which the value may no
  longer bear out, or in a new sentence with no value at all. A word inside
  an `if` or `sign` span is already guarded and is not listed.
- `if-zero`: an `if` condition that compares with zero.
- `lone-bar`: a bracket with one `|` and no governor, which is probably a
  span with a misspelt key.
- `name`: a class or key that weft does not know, especially one that is
  one edit from a weft name, such as `iff`.
- `long-guard`: an `if` arm longer than `guard_words` (25 words).
- `anchor-unused`, `xref-code`: an anchor nobody refers to, and a
  cross-reference written inside a code span.

Over a whole project the tier-2 rules can list a great deal. They are meant
for new material: `changes()` and `verify()` run them over the lines added
since a commit.

## Settings

| Setting | Default | Governs |
|---|---|---|
| `label_words` | `[]` | words after which a number is exempt |
| `numeral_years` | `false` | whether a four-digit year is exempt |
| `claim_words` | `{add: [], drop: []}` | words added to or dropped from the claim-word list |
| `claim_cap` | `20` | claim-word sentences listed per file before a count replaces them |
| `guard_words` | `25` | the length of an `if` arm that `long-guard` lists |
| `expected_names` | `[]` | classes (`.foo`) and keys (`foo`) from other tools that `name` should accept |
| `strict` | `[]` | tier-1 rules whose every instance fails `verify()` |
| `anchor_calls` | `[]` | helper calls that define anchors, for `xref`, `anchor-twice` and `anchor-unused` |

`strict` is for the end of adoption. Once a project has removed every typed
number, `strict: [numeral]` makes `verify()` fail on any that remain,
whether or not they were committed before.

## Anchors made by a helper

A project that makes its tables or figures with a helper, such as
`tbl(x, id = "depths")`, can tell the lints about it:

```yaml
anchor_calls:
  - fun: tbl
    arg: id
    prefix: "tbl-"
```

A call of `tbl()` in an executed R chunk, bare or as `pkg::tbl()`, then
defines the anchor `tbl-depths`, at the call's line, for `xref`,
`anchor-twice` and `anchor-unused`. `arg` is the name of the argument, or its
position when it is a whole number; `prefix` is optional. Only a literal
string counts: a computed id defines nothing, and no finding says so. An
entry without `fun` or `arg` is a configuration error.

## The two readers

By default the lints tell prose from code with weft's own reader, which runs
no Pandoc and gives the same answer on every machine. `lints(reader =
"pandoc")` also parses each document with Pandoc 3.0 or later, and counts a
character as prose only when both readers agree. It finds the Pandoc
version from the option `weft.pandoc`, the variable `WEFT_PANDOC`, Quarto,
rmarkdown or the path.
